newsitem.title: UK: UK Jan data show tight job mkt, prompt rate talk.
newsitem.headline: UK Jan data show tight job mkt, prompt rate talk.

text.p: A dramatic fall in UK unemployment in January confirmed tighter labour market conditions and will heighten concerns that rising wage demands will begin to force inflation higher in the near term, analysts said on Wednesday.
The data could present problems for the Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke as he seeks to fight off calls for higher interest rates to cool price pressures.
"The worst news for the government and money markets is the acceleration in underlying average earnings," said Jeremy Hawkins, senior economic advisor at Bank America.

"The labour market data are strong, and while unlikely to prompt a near-term tightening of policy, they will increase speculation that rates will have to be hiked immediately after the election," he said.

The jobs data showed unemployment fell by a seasonally -adjusted 67,800 in January -- more than double market expectations -- and that the jobless rate fell to 6.5 percent from 6.7 percent in December.
Underlying average earnings rose 4.25 percent in the year to December -- above market forecasts for a 4.0 percent rise.

"The news that average eranings growth has risen to 4.25 percent is unexpected and will support the Bank of England's call ... that interest rates should be modestly increased," said Andrew Milligan, economist at General Accident in London.
The Bank, which is due to publish its quarterly inflation report at 1130 GMT on Wednesday, is expected to reiterate the nedd for tighter credit.
But analysts said Clarke was likely to remain steadfast in his bid not to move base rates before the next election.
"Clarke's position has been set down," said David Coleman, chief economist at CIBC in London.
"It is pretty clear that he plans to hold out until after the election."

Analysts said that while the headline figures for unemployment and average earnings were worrying for gilts, certain factors in the report showed that weakness remained in some areas of the labour market.

They noted that the biggest rises in earnings were in production and manufacturing -- two of the weakest sectors in the economy at the moment -- while the earnings growth in the better-performing services sector was more subdued.
These factors will limit the downside for gilts, they said.
"You could make a case for both sides of the argument from these figures," said Coleman.
"But given that the market has been very strong recently on the basis that data have been quite weak, there is probably just enough concern in the jobs data for gilts to pull back a bit."

Jonathan Loynes, economist at HSBC Markets in London, also noted some weaker elements -- in particular unit wage costs, which rose 3.2 percent in the three months to December compared with a year earlier, down from 4.0 percent in November.
"The rise in earnings growth is disappointing, but as far as the inflation outlook is concerned, it is unit wage costs that matter," said Loynes. "And here the news in encouraging."
